text: Old Faithful's eruptions, with the data first, the closest bell curve is this one. Put the bell first, and if closeness works both ways, it stays at one, or does it move to two or three? The D stands for KL divergence, named for cullback and lie blur. Every maximum likelihood fit is the closest model by it, and it's often called a distance between distributions. So treat it as one. Data first, this bell is 0.76 bits away. Shift it or stretch it, and that number only grows, so this is bell A. Three and a half minutes give or take 1.1, but a distance reads the same both ways. Put the bell first, and the same two curves are 1.7 bits apart, more than twice as far. Only the order changed, so the order must be built into the formula. To see why, open it up at one real eruption, two minutes long. The data's curve gives that length a height, p. The bell gives it q, about a quarter as much. Double q twice and you reach p, so log base 2 of p over q is about 2. Two doublings or two bits. Do that at every length, then weight each one by how often eruptions last that long, which is p, and add it all up. Where the bell rises above the data, the gray dips pay a little back. That's the divergence, 0.76 bits. Try a bell that ignores the short eruptions and sits on the long hump. At two minutes, it falls short by 18 and a half doublings. More than a third of all eruptions are short ones like this so the bill comes to 5 bits Now keep that bill and swap the order for a second one Every P trades places with Q. The bell supplies the lengths and the data judges them. Which bell wins now? Take bell B first. It almost never imagines a short eruption, so ignoring them costs it nothing. It pays .62. Bell A imagines eruptions in the gap and out in the tails. Lengths the data almost never shows. That costs 1.7 bits. Now start from A and let the bell slide downhill on the bell-first bill. As that bill drains, the other one swells and the bell settles on the long hump, less than half as wide. Flip the order and the closest bell moves to 3. Maximum likelihood puts the data first, so its fits stretch over every hump. Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior with the model first, so it settles on one hump. Bly and colleagues note that variational inference, generally, underestimates posterior variance. Here, Bell B keeps only 15% of the posterior's variance. Settling on one hump needs that gap to be nearly empty. Smooth the data with R's default setting, and the gap fills enough that the best bell-first fit comes out wide. Smoothing chosen by cross-validation keeps the gap nearly empty and the fit on one hump. So closeness depends on which curve goes first. Bell A never misses an eruption that happens. Bell B almost never imagines one that doesn't.
